label: Reverse Glass Painting
defn: Folk pictures painted in reverse on the back of a glass pane, made in glassworks districts of Austria, Bavaria and Bohemia from the 18th century and sold at fairs and shrines: Sandl devotional pictures with the Sandl rose, saints and Madonnas for the home altar.
note: West slice holds the Alpine/Danubian folk tradition; eastern glass icons are a seam with europe_folk_east

label: Duodji
defn: The handicraft of the Sámi of Norway, Sweden, Finland and the Kola peninsula, divided into hard duodji (antler, bone and wood) and soft duodji (leather, textiles and pewter-thread embroidery): antler-handled knives, carved drinking cups (guksi), pewter-thread embroidered bags.
note: placed in D2 because carved antler and bone is its core; soft duodji is a kind group

label: Processional Giants
defn: Huge carried effigies of giants, animals and dragons, built of wicker, wood and papier-mâché and paraded at town festivals of the Low Countries, northern France and Iberia: gegants of Catalonia, giants of Flanders and Wallonia, Jas de Keistamper of Boxtel.

label: Estremoz Clay Figures
defn: Small modelled and painted clay figures of Estremoz in the Alentejo, made since the 17th century, first for nativity scenes and then of saints and rural types in regional dress: presépios, Primavera, Amor é cego.
aliases: Bonecos de Estremoz;figurado de barro de Estremoz

label: Gákti
defn: The dress of the Sámi, a tunic of wool or reindeer skin trimmed with woven bands and coloured cloth whose cut and colours mark region and family: Kautokeino gákti, four-winds hat.

label: Bunad
defn: The regional folk costumes of Norway, revived and standardised from local dress since the late 19th century, with embroidered bodices, aprons and silver brooches (sølje): Vest-Telemark bunad, Hardanger bunad.
see: L7 Swedish Folk Costume;L8 Tracht;L10 Hardanger Embroidery

label: Swedish Folk Costume
defn: The parish costumes of Sweden, worn and revived as signs of local and national identity, with embroidered bodices, pockets and headdresses: Dalarna costumes, Leksand and Rättvik dress.
note: Dalarna and Nås costume rows were excluded below the inclusion rule

label: Tracht
defn: The regional folk dress of the German-speaking Alps and southern Germany, made and worn in local forms with their own headdresses, bodices and embroidery: Bregenzerwald Juppe, Lake Constance Radhaube, Gailtal costume.

label: Greek Island Embroidery
defn: The silk-on-linen embroidery of the Aegean and Ionian islands and Epirus (17th–19th century), each island with its own stitches and designs, used for bed curtains, cushions and dress: Cretan skirt borders, Rhodian bed tents, Naxos and Dodecanese hangings.
note: Met-collection study; Ashmolean "Aegean Legacies" also uses the term; lace is a kind group

label: Hardanger Embroidery
defn: Norwegian whitework of counted satin-stitch blocks (kloster) with cut and drawn threads, from the Hardanger district, used on bunad aprons and linens.

label: Mountmellick Embroidery
defn: Irish white embroidery of raised floral designs in thick cotton on white cotton satin, begun in Mountmellick, County Laois, about 1825 by Johanna Carter.

label: Arraiolos Rug
defn: Portuguese wool rugs embroidered in Slav (long-armed cross) stitch on linen or jute canvas, made in Arraiolos in the Alentejo since the 17th century.
note: needlework rug: H4 by technique, not H1

label: Bordados da Glória do Ribatejo
defn: The embroidery of Glória do Ribatejo (Salvaterra de Magos), worked mainly in cross stitch on household linens and local dress.

label: Alençon Lace
defn: French needle lace of Alençon in Normandy, developed in the 1660s under royal patronage and made into the 19th century, with fine réseau ground and corded outlines: flounces, lappets.

label: Burano Lace
defn: Venetian needle lace of the island of Burano, revived in 1872 by the Burano lace school on the model of the old Venetian points.
note: enwiki redirect goes to Argentella; QID used

label: Lefkara Lace
defn: The drawn-thread and needle-lace embroidery of Pano Lefkara in Cyprus, worked on linen in geometric designs (UNESCO 2009).

label: Brussels Lace
defn: Pillow lace of Brussels and Brabant, its motifs made separately in bobbin or needle lace and joined to a droschel or bride ground (17th–19th century), including point de gaze and Brussels appliqué.

label: Mechlin Lace
defn: Flemish bobbin lace of Mechelen with a hexagonal ground and a flat thread outlining the motifs, the 18th century's favourite lace for ruffles.

label: Quill Embroidery
defn: Embroidery of leather with split quills of peacock tail feathers on belts, braces and shoes of Alpine dress, practised in Tyrol (Sarntal) and Austria.

label: Honiton Lace
defn: English bobbin lace of east Devon whose motifs are made separately and joined, famed for Queen Victoria's wedding lace (1840).

label: Le Puy Lace
defn: Bobbin lace of Le Puy-en-Velay in the Auvergne, in linen, silk and wool guipures and Cluny-style laces made by cottage lacemakers.

label: Maltese Lace
defn: Bobbin lace of Malta and Gozo, above all the 19th-century silk guipure with the Maltese cross and wheatears.

label: Headford Lace
defn: The bobbin lace of Headford, County Galway, a cottage industry of the 18th–19th centuries revived today.

label: Carrickmacross Lace
defn: Irish appliqué lace of County Monaghan, cambric shapes cut and sewn on machine net, introduced about 1820 by Mrs Grey Porter.
see: L25 Limerick Lace;L26 Irish Crochet Lace

label: Limerick Lace
defn: Irish embroidered net lace of Limerick (from 1829), worked in tambour (chain stitch) or run (darning) stitch on machine net.

label: Irish Crochet Lace
defn: Crochet made in imitation of Venetian needle lace, spread as famine relief from the 1840s; motifs are worked separately and joined with a crocheted mesh: Clones lace, Youghal-area crochet.

label: Blaudruck
defn: Resist block printing and indigo dyeing of linen and cotton, carried on by family dye-works of Central Europe (UNESCO 2018, Austria, Czechia, Germany, Hungary, Slovakia): Burgenland blueprint, Mühlviertel indigo printing.
note: multinational; East slice may hold its centres as kinds

label: Staphorster Stipwerk
defn: Dot printing of Staphorst in Overijssel: coloured patterns stamped with pin-headed stamps on cloth for the village dress (kraplap, caps).

label: Freest Fisherman's Carpets
defn: Knotted carpets designed and made since the 1920s on the coast of the Bay of Greifswald (Freest, Western Pomerania), with motifs of fish, birds and sea.

label: Panier de Mayun
defn: The willow and bramble baskets of Mayun in the Brière marshes (Loire-Atlantique).

label: Bastabinne
defn: Swedish baskets plaited from strips of spruce bast.

label: Talavera de la Reina Pottery
defn: Tin-glazed earthenware of Talavera de la Reina and El Puente del Arzobispo in Castile from the 16th century, in blue-and-white and polychrome, for tableware, apothecary jars and tile panels (UNESCO 2019, with Puebla): serie tricolor, Puente del Arzobispo green-and-ochre ware.

label: Bisalhães Black Pottery
defn: Black earthenware of Bisalhães near Vila Real, burnished and fired in a smothered pit kiln (soenga), for cooking and decoration (UNESCO urgent safeguarding 2016).

label: Gmundner Keramik
defn: Earthenware of Gmunden on the Traunsee, made since the 15th century, best known for its 'flamed' (geflammt) slip decoration in green, blue or brown.

label: Émaux de Longwy
defn: Faience of Longwy in Lorraine decorated since the 1870s with coloured enamels filled into printed outlines in the manner of cloisonné.

label: Rhenish Stoneware
defn: Salt-glazed stoneware of the Rhineland centres (Siegburg, Raeren, Frechen, Cologne, Westerwald), 15th–19th century, exported across Europe and its colonies: Bartmann (Bellarmine) jugs, Westerwald blue-and-grey tankards.
note: Met and V&A use the term; no enwiki article (Westerwald pottery has one)

label: Art of Glass Beads
defn: Venetian and French lampwork and drawn glass beadmaking (perle veneziane), inscribed by UNESCO in 2020 for Italy and France.
note: label is the UNESCO element name

label: Hairwork
defn: Jewellery and pictures worked from human hair, a 19th-century fashion carried on as a village craft in Vamhus, Dalarna.
note: in G3 by function (worn as ornament)
